newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan refiners expected to keep crude runs low.
newsitem.headline: Japan refiners expected to keep crude runs low.

text.p: Japanese refiners are likely to maintain their policy of keeping crude runs low for the rest of this year in an attempt to support domestic oil product prices by keeping supplies tight, oil industry sources said.

"Refiners' policy of keeping throughput and stockpiles low in order to support oil product prices is expected to continue," Takashi Kawai, an analyst with private think-tank Nikko Research Centre, said.
"The lower runs last winter were effective in pushing wholesale prices up," an official with a refiner said.
"I expect most refiners to keep runs low," he said.

Crude throughput during April to June this year averaged 3.74 million barrels per day (bpd), which in terms of refinery utilisation rates comes to 71 percent, according to the Petroleum Association of Japan.
This represents a decline of 2.2 points compared to 73.2 percent during the same period a year earlier.
Japan's total processing capacity is currently 5.3 million barrels per stream day (BPSD).

"Plans are to keep throughput a little below last year's levels," an official with a second refinery said. "Throughput last winter turned out to be higher than initial plans as temperatures were colder than expected," he said.
In 1995, operating rates during July to September were 77.3 percent, and 79.5 percent during October to December.
Japanese oil company officials also cited the industry's need to trim storage costs by keeping inventories at low levels.
Japan's oil industry has been exposed to more competition since restrictions on oil product imports were lifted in April, which has forced companies to take steps to cut costs.
Before deregulation, imports of oil products, such as gasoline, gas oil and kerosene, were restricted to refiners. Now non-refiners with the proper facilities can make imports.
"Previously refiners held surplus stockpiles, feeling an obligation to provide (the public with) a stable supply," an official with a refinery said.
"However, with the deregulation in imports, we no longer feel it our responsibility (to secure a stable supply). We cannot afford to carry on costly practices," he said.
In Japan, all refiners and importers must hold a minimum of 70 days supply of crude or oil products. Separately from this, refiners maintain their own product stockpiles.

In order to maintain a competitive edge over imports, major refiners introduced a new wholesale pricing system this year which aims to bring domestic oil product prices in line with the international market.

This means increasing kerosene and gas oil prices while lowering those of gasoline, although efforts to raise kerosene and gas oil prices have met strong opposition from consumer groups and truck drivers.
"With price talks between refiners and buyers on kerosene just about to start, it is hard to imagine refiners will boost runs and increase supplies," analyst Kawai said.
"Oil product stockpiles this winter may not be built up to match last year's levels," he said.

In Japan, crude throughput is normally lowest during April to June due to a wave of refinery turnarounds, but increases towards the winter as refiners start building stockpiles of kerosene, used for heating.

Processing peaks during January to March with kerosene demand. Throughput during this period is also boosted by refiners' need to build oil product stockpiles ahead of regular refinery maintenance checks.
